Memory? No, no, my memory is just fine. I never have trouble finding the right word. In fact, I do the crossword puzzle every single morning, in pen. Though I'll tell you, the clues they put in there lately... it's a completely different language. Half of them are about these new pop singers or computer gadgets. Yesterday they wanted a four-letter word for some internet thing. How on earth am I supposed to know that? 

It's just like the slang the kids use now. Mary's grand-niece was over here a few weeks back, and she kept saying everything was "sick." I asked her if she needed a thermometer! She just laughed at me. She brought over a green bean casserole, actually. But she used fresh green beans instead of the canned ones. Now, you might think fresh is better, but for a casserole, you really need that softness you only get from the tin. Plus, she completely forgot the crispy onions on top. It's not a proper green bean casserole without the French's onions. I went to buy a can of them at the market just last week, and they've shrunk the tin! Same price, mind you, but half the onions. It's highway robbery. The young man at the register didn't even care when I pointed it out, just kept chewing his gum. 

But what was the question? Oh, forgetting things. No, I remember everything perfectly well. No trouble with that.

Strange beliefs? No, nothing like that. I don't believe in ghosts or aliens or anyone trying to harm me. My head is screwed on straight. 

Though, speaking of strange beliefs, you wouldn't believe the absolute nonsense they put on the television now. Just fine.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any days when you didn't feel like doing even the things you usually enjoy, like tinkering in the garage or sitting on the porch with Mary?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I always find my way out to the garage eventually. Though, I tell you, yesterday I couldn't find my good wood glue to save my life. I've had this one bottle for... oh, it's got to be five years. The kind with the orange cap, you know? They used to make it different, much thicker. Now it's practically water. \n\nIt's just like everything else they make these days. They put up these new group mailboxes down our street last month, supposed to be secure and weatherproof or some nonsense. I always have plenty to keep me occupied.\n\nDoctor: Over the past few weeks, have you had days where you felt little pleasure or interest in things, even the things you usually enjoy?\n\nPatient: Didn't we just... well, no, I haven't lost interest in anything. I still enjoy my routine just fine. Every morning I sit and read the paper, cover to cover. It's just a complete lack of pride in one's work, that's what it is. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Believed something strongly that others didn't? No, no, I've never been one of those stubborn types who won't listen to reason. If I'm wrong, I'm wrong. 

But you know who was stubborn? My brother-in-law, Arthur. God rest his soul. Arthur was convinced, absolutely convinced, that the moon landing was filmed in a basement in Nevada. We'd sit around the dinner table at Thanksgiving, and he'd start going on about the shadows in the photographs and the flag waving in the breeze. My sister Margaret would just roll her eyes and pass the gravy. She made the best gravy, Margaret did. Always used the drippings from the turkey, never that powdered stuff from a packet. I don't understand people who use the packets. It takes five extra minutes to make a proper roux. 

I was at the supermarket yesterday, actually, looking for a good roasting chicken, and the prices! You'd think the chickens were laying golden eggs. I asked the butcher—not the old butcher, Mr. Klein, he retired to Arizona two years ago, it's a young kid now with tattoos all up his arms. I asked him why a simple bird costs as much as a steak dinner used to, and he just shrugged and mumbled something about supply chains. Supply chains! In my day, the supply chain was the farmer down the road bringing his truck to the market on Tuesday mornings. You knew exactly where your food came from. 

Now everything comes wrapped in three layers of plastic from halfway across the world. It's terrible for the environment, all that plastic. I try to recycle, I really do, but they keep changing the rules. One week you can put the glass in with the paper, the next week they leave a nasty little sticker on your bin saying you've done it all wrong. How's a person supposed to keep track? 

But what were you asking? Oh, about believing things that aren't true. No, I don't have any problem with that. I just stick to the facts.

No, no, I don't think so. I've always been pretty level-headed about things. If someone shows me I'm wrong, well, I'll admit it.

Doc, are you... are you pulling my leg here? Or is this some kind of memory test for you? Because I swear on my mother's grave you just asked me that. For the fourth time! No. The answer is still no. I don't believe things that aren't true, and I don't need people showing me proof of anything.

Doc, I swear you are trying to test my blood pressure today. Something bad happening? No. I don't sit around waiting for the boogeyman to jump out of the closet. I don't get spooked for no reason. 

Although, you want to talk about something bad actually happening, you should've seen the basement of my first house back in the spring of '93. Now that was a disaster, and I had plenty of reason to be worried then! We had a sump pump, a big cast-iron thing, weighed about fifty pounds. They built things to last back then, or so I thought. Anyway, Bob said it was just a spring shower. Next thing I know, I'm standing in two feet of muddy water, trying to rescue my wife's sewing machine.

But, uh, anyway. What was the question? Bad things happening? No, no, I don't worry about things like that unless I'm standing in two feet of water. I really think we've beaten this horse to death, Doc. Can we please turn the page on your little notepad now?

I don't understand people who use the packets. Doc, I... I just don't understand. Are you deaf? Or is the battery dying in my hearing aid? Because I could have sworn I just answered this exact same question three times already! No! I don't go around believing things without proof!

I try to recycle, I really do, but they keep changing the rules. One week you can put the glass in with the paper, the next week they leave a nasty little sticker on your bin saying you've done it all wrong. How's a person supposed to keep track? \n\nBut what were you asking? Oh, about believing things that aren't true. No, I don't have any problem with that. I just stick to the facts.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever believed something very strongly that turned out not to be true, even when other people tried to tell you otherwise?\n\nPatient: No, no, I don't think so. I've always been pretty level-headed about things. If someone shows me I'm wrong, well, I'll admit it. \n\nThough, you know, my neighbor, Tom—he lives two doors down in that blue house with the overgrown hedges—he was absolutely convinced that the city was going to widen our street. He was out there measuring his front lawn every afternoon, muttering about eminent domain and property values. I told him, \"Tom, they haven't even filled the pothole at the corner of Elm and Maple in three years, they're not going to pave over your prized petunias.\" \n\nAnd speaking of petunias, the deer this year have been absolutely ruthless. I put up that netting, you know, the black plastic kind that's supposed to be invisible? Well, it's invisible to me, because I tripped right over it watering the hostas on Tuesday. But the deer? They just push right under it. It's like a buffet for them. I tried that spray, the one that smells like rotten eggs and garlic. Cost me fourteen dollars at the garden center. Fourteen dollars! And it washed right off in the rain on Thursday. \n\nWe used to have a dog, a golden retriever named Buster, and he'd chase the deer right out of the yard. Best dog you could ask for. He loved to ride in the car, head out the window, ears flapping. We'd take him up to the lake every summer. The water used to be so clear up there, you could see the bottom even in the deep end. Now, I hear they have problems with that algae. It's a shame, really. \n\nBut anyway, what was it you were asking? Oh, about believing things that aren't true. No, I don't think I've ever had that problem. I just take things as they are.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been absolutely certain of something that turned out not to be true, even when people close to you tried to tell you otherwise?\n\nPatient: Doc, I feel like we're going in circles here. Are you sure you're not the one getting mixed up? You've asked me this three times now! No, I don't get confused about what's real and what isn't. \n\nYou're starting to sound a bit like that old grandfather clock I have in the front hallway, just chiming the same note over and over. I actually had to have a fellow come out and look at that clock last month. The pendulum was swinging just fine, but the hands wouldn't move past quarter to four. He was a nice enough guy, wore one of those little magnifying glasses over his eye—a loupe, I think they call it. He told me the mainspring was shot. Cost me an absolute fortune to get it replaced. \n\nYou can't just go to the hardware store for parts like that anymore. Nobody knows how to fix anything mechanical. Everything is digital now. My grandson, he has a watch that doesn't even have hands. It just lights up and tells him how many steps he takes in a day. Why on earth do you need a machine to tell you how many steps you've taken? You walk until you get where you're going, and then you sit down! He was tapping on the face of it all through dinner last Sunday, completely ignoring his mother. I tell you, if I had done something like that at the dinner table when my father was around... well, let's just say you wouldn't do it twice. He was a strict man, my father. Worked at the steel mill for forty-two years. Never missed a shift. \n\nBut... wait, did I answer your question? You were asking about being certain of things that aren't true. Yeah, no, I definitely don't have that issue. Like I said, my head is on straight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever believed something very strongly that turned out to be completely untrue, even when there was clear evidence against it or everyone else told you you were wrong?\n\nPatient: Doc, is there an echo in this office? I swear you're just reading the exact same question off that clipboard again. I told you, no. I don't get mixed up like that. I know what's true and what isn't. \n\nBut speaking of repeating things... my wife's sister, Martha, she used to have this bird. A cockatiel or a parrot, something with a little yellow tuft on its head. Nasty little bird named Captain. All day long, it would just squawk, \"Where's the remote? Where's the remote?\" Because Martha was always losing the television clicker. She'd leave it in the refrigerator, under the couch cushions... I think once I found it in the flour canister when I was over there trying to make a batch of biscuits. \n\nI make a wonderful buttermilk biscuit, you know. The secret is ice-cold butter. You have to grate it in with a cheese grater. Most people just mash it with a fork, but grating it is what gives you those flaky layers. I tried to show my grand-niece how to do it last Christmas, but she was too busy staring at her phone. Nobody learns how to cook from scratch anymore. They just use those apps on their phones where a complete stranger leaves a soggy paper bag of food on your front porch. It's ridiculous, if you ask me. You don't know whose kitchen that came from! They could have a cat walking all over the counters for all you know. \n\nBut, uh... wait, what was the question? Something about evidence? No, like I said before, I don't believe in fairy tales. I'm perfectly fine.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been completely sure of something that wasn’t true, even when people showed you proof that it wasn’t?\n\nPatient: Doc, are you... are you pulling my leg here? Or is this some kind of memory test for you? Because I swear on my mother's grave you just asked me that. For the fourth time! No. The answer is still no. I don't believe things that aren't true, and I don't need people showing me proof of anything. \n\nYou're just like my old 68 Chevy truck, just crank, crank, crank, turning over but never catching. Lord, that truck hated the cold. I had to go out there every morning in January with a can of starter fluid. You'd take the air cleaner off, spray it right down the throat of the carburetor. Try doing that with a car today! You can't. It's all fuel injected, sealed up under a big plastic cover. It's all computers now. My neighbor, the one with the petunias I was telling you about, he took his car to the dealership last month because a little light on the dashboard came on. Cost him four hundred dollars just for them to plug a laptop into his dashboard and tell him a sensor was dusty. Four hundred dollars! I told him, Tom, in 1972 I rebuilt a whole transmission for less than that. My buddy Frank and I, we spent a whole Labor Day weekend pulling the engine out of his Pontiac, grease up to our elbows... \n\nBut, uh, anyway. What were we saying? Proof. Right. No, nobody has to show me proof of anything because I don't get crazy ideas in my head to begin with. I think we can safely move on to the next question on your clipboard now, don't you?\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had any strong suspicions or beliefs about something happening in your life — like someone trying to cheat you, follow you, or do you harm — that turned out not to be true, even though you were very sure of it at the time?\n\nPatient: Are you... are you sure you're feeling alright today, Doc? Because now you're asking me the same thing, just with different words! No, I don't think people are trying to cheat me or follow me around. I'm not some secret agent. I'm just an old man trying to get by.\n\nSpeaking of getting by, though, did I tell you they raised the price of stamps again? It's absolute robbery. I went down to the post office on Elm Street—the one with the brass handles on the doors, they don't make doors like that anymore—just to mail my electric bill. I still write a check, you know. Put it in an envelope, stick a stamp on it. The girl behind the counter, she had purple hair. Purple! Like a plum. I didn't say anything, of course, it's not my place, but back in my day, if you showed up to a government job with purple hair, they'd send you right back home to wash it out. Anyway, she tells me it's going to cost me nearly a dollar just to mail a single envelope. A dollar! I remember when you could send a letter across the country for three cents. And the mailman actually walked up to your porch. Our mailman, Mr. Henderson, he knew everybody on the block. He'd even carry dog biscuits in his pocket for the strays. \n\nNow they just drive up in those little white trucks with the steering wheel on the wrong side, shove a bunch of junk mail in the box at the end of the driveway, and speed off. Half the time they give me the neighbor's coupons. I don't need coupons for cat food, I don't even own a cat! I had a dog once, a Golden Retriever named Buster. Smartest dog you ever saw. He could balance a tennis ball on his nose for a full minute...\n\nBut, uh, where was I going with that? Oh, right. Cheating and following and all that nonsense. No, nothing like that. Nobody's out to get me. Can we talk about something else now? I feel like a broken record.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a strong belief about something that others told you wasn't true, but you still felt certain about it, even if there was no proof to support it?\n\nPatient: Doc, I... I really don't know what to tell you anymore. Are you writing a book on this or something? Because I feel like I'm taking crazy pills just sitting here listening to you ask the same thing five different ways. No. I don't have strong beliefs about things that aren't true. I don't need proof, and I don't argue with people about things that aren't real. \n\nAlthough, speaking of arguing, you should have seen the row my brother and I got into back in '85 over a lawnmower. It was a Toro, red, self-propelled. Beautiful machine. I lent it to him for the weekend because his grass was getting up past his ankles, and he brings it back with the blade bent like a pretzel. Said he hit a rock. A rock! In his yard? The man's lawn was practically a golf course, not a pebble in sight. I told him he must have run over a piece of rebar or something, but he swore up and down it was just a rock. We didn't speak for three months over that mower. \n\nHe ended up buying me a new blade, finally. We went down to the hardware store—Miller's Hardware, it used to be right on the corner of 4th and Main, before they tore it down to build that awful strip mall with the frozen yogurt place. Who eats frozen yogurt anyway? It's just ice cream that's trying to trick you into thinking it's healthy. If I'm going to eat dessert, I want a real bowl of ice cream. Butter pecan. My wife used to make a homemade peach ice cream in the summer. We had one of those old wooden crank machines, you had to pack the rock salt and the ice all around the sides... took forever, and your arm would be aching by the time it was done, but lord, it was the best thing you ever tasted. \n\nBut... what were we talking about? The lawnmower? No, you were asking about beliefs or something. Like I said, Doc, no. I'm a very practical man. I deal with the facts, and that's it. Can we please, please move on to something else?\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt that something bad was going to happen to you, even when there was no real reason to think so?\n\nPatient: Doc, I swear you are trying to test my blood pressure today. Something bad happening? No. I don't sit around waiting for the boogeyman to jump out of the closet. I don't get spooked for no reason. \n\nAlthough, you want to talk about something bad actually happening, you should've seen the basement of my first house back in the spring of '93. Now that was a disaster, and I had plenty of reason to be worried then! We had a sump pump, a big cast-iron thing, weighed about fifty pounds. They built things to last back then, or so I thought. We got three days of heavy rain—just torrential, coming down sideways. The weatherman, old Bob Jenkins on Channel 4, he always wore those loud plaid suits, you remember him? Anyway, Bob said it was just a spring shower. Next thing I know, I'm standing in two feet of muddy water, trying to rescue my wife's sewing machine. \n\nIt was a Singer, a beautiful heavy thing with the gold filigree on the side. She used to make all the curtains for the house. You go to a store now, and the curtains are all thin, cheap polyester, made in who-knows-where, and they charge you an arm and a leg for 'em. My wife would go down to the fabric store and spend hours just feeling the cottons and the linens. She made this one set for the living room, a nice heavy brocade, blocked out the sun completely so I could watch the Sunday game without a glare on the television. Televisions used to have real glass screens, you know, not these flat little plastic things you hang on the wall like a picture frame...\n\nBut, uh, anyway. What was the question? Bad things happening? No, no, I don't worry about things like that unless I'm standing in two feet of water. I really think we've beaten this horse to death, Doc. Can we please turn the page on your little notepad now?\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been absolutely convinced of something that wasn’t true, even when people showed you clear proof that it wasn’t?\n\nPatient: Doc, is this a joke? Is there a hidden camera in here somewhere? Because I feel like I'm stuck in that movie, the one with the groundhog. You are asking me the exact same question again, just shuffling the words around! Anyway, I was convinced I knew a shortcut through South Dakota. She had the Rand McNally atlas out—you remember those? The big spiral-bound ones you kept under the passenger seat. I don't have the CIA tapping my phone. \n\nI mean, the only thing my neighbor is plotting is how to let his dog ruin my garden. He lets him out in the morning and the darn thing comes right over and digs up my beefsteak tomatoes. \n\nYou can't even grow a decent tomato these days anyway, not like you used to. Back when I was a kid, my mother grew tomatoes the size of softballs. We'd slice 'em thick, put a little mayonnaise on white bread, maybe some salt and pepper... best sandwich you ever had in your life. You buy a tomato at the supermarket now, it's pale pink and tastes like wet cardboard. They pick 'em green, you see, and gas 'em in the trucks to turn 'em red. It’s a crying shame. My mother used to spend all of August canning them. We had a cellar full of Mason jars. You had to boil the lids just right so they’d pop and seal, otherwise the whole batch would spoil... \n\nBut... what were you saying? The government? Doc, listen to me very carefully. Nobody is watching me. Nobody is plotting against me. I am just an old man trying to grow a decent tomato. I don't go around believing things without proof! \n\nThe only people who believe things without proof are the ones buying junk off those late-night infomercials. You know the ones. I couldn't sleep one night, oh, must have been back in '98, maybe '99. My knee was acting up. So I'm sitting in the living room in my recliner—it was a La-Z-Boy, a real nice corduroy one, olive green. They don't make the fabric like that anymore, you know. Now it's all that fake leather that peels off in little flakes and gets all over the carpet. You spend half your Sunday just running the Hoover over it. \n\nAnyway, I turn on the television, and there's this fella selling a copper bracelet. He says it cures arthritis, aligns your magnets or some nonsense. He had a voice just like Robert Stack. You remember Robert Stack? From Unsolved Mysteries? Man, that show used to give me the absolute creeps. That spooky theme music... they’d show those police sketches of bank robbers and I'd be looking out my front window for a week thinking every guy walking down the street in a trench coat was on the FBI's most wanted list. Trench coats used to be very popular, you know. Humphrey Bogart wore one, and suddenly every guy taking the train to the office thought he was a private eye. You don't see men wearing proper hats or coats anymore, just those hooded sweatshirts... \n\nBut look, what are we even doing here, Doc? I told you, no. No false beliefs. No crazy ideas without proof. I'm sane. I'm bored, and I'm getting pretty irritated, but I'm sane. Now, are you going to check my heart rate or should I just go home and watch the game?\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been completely certain of something that wasn't true, even after seeing clear proof that it wasn't real or others showed you otherwise?\n\nPatient: Doc, I swear to you, you are a broken record. Are you doing this on purpose? Speaking of broken records, we used to have this big Zenith console stereo in the living room. Beautiful piece of furniture, solid walnut. Took up half the wall. You had to let the tubes warm up for a minute before it would even play a sound. I'd stack up the records on the spindle—Sinatra, mostly, maybe some Nat King Cole. \n\nPeople don't listen to real singers anymore. Now it's just thump-thump-thump noise. You can feel it rattling your teeth when a car drives by. Kids today are going to ruin their hearing. My grandson, he walks around with those little white plugs shoved in his ears from morning till night. I asked him once, how do you hear the birds? Or a fire engine coming down the street? He just shrugged at me. Kids don't pay attention to the world around them anymore. When I was a boy, we were outside until the streetlights came on. We'd play stickball in the alley, and if you broke a window, you'd better believe you were working all summer to pay for it. Now they just sit on the couch staring at screens...\n\nWait, why am I talking about my grandson? Oh, for the love of Pete. You asked me the exact same thing again! No! I am completely certain that I do NOT believe things that aren't true. I don't need proof, I don't need evidence, I just need you to ask me a different question! My blood pressure has got to be through the roof right now. Can you check that? Let's check that instead of playing this little game!"
